article.title: Robots and us
glossary: * terraforming: modifying a planet's atmosphere to suit human needs
* singularity: the point when robots will be able to start creating ever more sophisticated versions of themselves

items.sentence_raw: When asked "Should robots be used to colonise other planets?", cosmology and astrophysics Professor Martin Rees said he believed the solar system would be mapped by robotic craft by the end of the century.
"The next step would be mining of asteroids, enabling fabrication of large structures in space without having to bring all the raw materials from Earth....
I think this is more realistic and benign than the... "terraforming"* of planets."
items.explain: Q34: Rees disapproves of *'terraforming'* (changing planets for human use), and Richardson thinks colonising other planets is morally wrong. **'Changes made to other planets for our own benefit'** covers both terraforming and colonisation ethical concerns. The answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: He maintains that colonised planets "should be preserved with a status that is analogous to Antarctica here on Earth."

On the question of using robots to colonise other planets and exploit mineral resources, engineering Professor Daniel Wolpert replied, "I don't see a pressing need to colonise other planets unless we can bring [these] resources back to Earth.
The vast majority of Earth is currently inaccessible to us.
Using robots to gather resources nearer to home would seem to be a better use of our robotic tools."
items.explain: Q31: Daniel Wolpert states *'Using robots to gather resources nearer to home would seem to be a better use of our robotic tools'*. **'Nearer to home'** means on Earth, not in space, so this matches the question idea. The answer is **B (Daniel Wolpert)**.

items.sentence_raw: Meanwhile, for anthropology Professor Kathleen Richardson, the idea of 'colonisation' of other planets seemed morally dubious: "I think whether we do something on Earth or on Mars we should always do it in the spirit of a genuine interest in "the Other", not to impose a particular model, but to meet 'the Other'."
items.explain: Q34: Rees disapproves of *'terraforming'* (changing planets for human use), and Richardson thinks colonising other planets is morally wrong. **'Changes made to other planets for our own benefit'** covers both terraforming and colonisation ethical concerns. The answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: In response to the second question, 'How soon will machine intelligence outstrip human intelligence?', Rees mentions robots that are advanced enough to beat humans at chess, but then goes on to say, "Robots are still limited in their ability to sense their environment: they can't yet recognise and move the pieces on a real chessboard as cleverly as a child can.
items.explain: Q35: Rees says robots already beat humans at chess but have limited environmental sense, and Wolpert says machine intelligence *'already has [outstripped humans] in a limited sense'*. Both talk about how far machine intelligence has developed up to now. The answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Later this century, however, their more advanced successors may relate to their surroundings, and to people, as adeptly as we do.
Moral questions then arise....
items.explain: Q30: Martin Rees asks in the passage *'Should we feel guilty about exploiting sophisticated robots?'*. **'Treating robots fairly'** in the question is exactly the moral issue this question refers to. The answer is **A (Martin Rees)**.

items.sentence_raw: Should we feel guilty about exploiting [sophisticated robots]?
items.explain: Q30: Martin Rees asks in the passage *'Should we feel guilty about exploiting sophisticated robots?'*. **'Treating robots fairly'** in the question is exactly the moral issue this question refers to. The answer is **A (Martin Rees)**.

items.sentence_raw: Should we fret if they are underemployed, frustrated, or bored?"
Wolpert's response to the question about machine intelligence outstripping human intelligence was this: "In a limited sense it already has.
items.explain: Q35: Rees says robots already beat humans at chess but have limited environmental sense, and Wolpert says machine intelligence *'already has [outstripped humans] in a limited sense'*. Both talk about how far machine intelligence has developed up to now. The answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Machines can already navigate, remember and search for items with an ability that far outstrips humans.
However, there is no machine that can identify visual objects or speech with the reliability and flexibility of humans....
Expecting a machine close to the creative intelligence of a human within the next 50 years would be highly ambitious."
items.explain: Q29: Daniel Wolpert says in the passage *'Expecting a machine close to the creative intelligence of a human within the next 50 years would be highly ambitious'*. **'Imaginative'** in the question means **'creative'**, and 50 years counts as *'many decades'*. The answer is **B (Daniel Wolpert)**.

items.sentence_raw: Richardson believes that our fear of machines becoming too advanced has more to do with human nature than anything intrinsic to the machines themselves.

In her view, it stems from humans' tendency to personify inanimate objects: we create machines based on representations of ourselves, imagine that machines think and behave as we do, and therefore see them as an autonomous threat.
items.explain: Q37: The passage says Richardson believes fear of machines *'stems from humans' tendency to personify inanimate objects'*. **'Attribute human characteristics to non-human entities'** is exactly what **'personify'** means. ***Option C is a trap*** — the fear comes from giving machines human traits, not misunderstanding how objects work. The answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: "One of the consequences of thinking that the problem lies with machines is that...
we tend to imagine they are greater and more powerful than they really are and subsequently they become so."
This led on to the third question, 'Should we be scared by advances in artificial intelligence?'
To this question, Rees replied, "Those who should be worried are the futurologists who believe in the so-called 'singularity'*....

And another worry is that we are increasingly dependent on computer networks, and that these could behave like a single 'brain' with a mind of its own, and with goals that may be contrary to human welfare.
items.explain: Q38: Rees says he worries computer networks *'could behave like a single brain with a mind of its own, and with goals that may be contrary to human welfare'*. **'Independent thought'** in option C matches *'a mind of its own'*. The answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: I think we should ensure that robots remain as no more than 'idiot savants' lacking the capacity to outwit us, even though they may greatly surpass us in the ability to calculate and process information."
items.explain: Q27: The passage says Martin Rees stated we *'should ensure that robots remain as no more than idiot savants lacking the capacity to outwit us'*. **'Restrict the abilities of robots'** in the question has the same meaning as this quote. The answer is **A (Martin Rees)**.

items.sentence_raw: Wolpert's response was to say that we have already seen the damaging effects of artificial intelligence in the form of computer viruses.
items.explain: Q36: Wolpert says we have already seen *'damaging effects of artificial intelligence in the form of computer viruses'*, but Richardson says no AI has ever challenged human supremacy. They disagree about whether existing AI has already caused harm. The answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: "But in this case," he says, "the real intelligence is the malicious designer.
Critically, the benefits of computers outweigh the damage that computer viruses cause.
Similarly, while there may be misuses of robotics in the near future, the benefits that they will bring are likely to outweigh these negative aspects."
Richardson's response to this question was this: "We need to ask why fears of artificial intelligence and robots persist; none have in fact risen up and challenged human supremacy."
items.explain: Q36: Wolpert says we have already seen *'damaging effects of artificial intelligence in the form of computer viruses'*, but Richardson says no AI has ever challenged human supremacy. They disagree about whether existing AI has already caused harm. The answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: She believes that as robots have never shown themselves to be a threat to humans, it seems unlikely that they ever will.
items.explain: Q28: Kathleen Richardson says in the passage *'robots have never shown themselves to be a threat to humans, it seems unlikely that they ever will'*. **'Less serious than humans believe'** matches this idea that the risk is not real or high. The answer is **C (Kathleen Richardson)**.

items.sentence_raw: In fact, she went on, "Not all fear [robots]; many people welcome machine intelligence."
items.explain: Q33: Kathleen Richardson says *'Not all fear robots; many people welcome machine intelligence'*. **'Look forward to robots developing greater intelligence'** is exactly what *'welcome machine intelligence'* means. The answer is **C (Kathleen Richardson)**.

items.sentence_raw: In answer to the fourth question, 'What can science fiction tell us about robotics?', Rees replied, "I sometimes advise students that it's better to read first-rate science fiction than second-rate science - more stimulating, and perhaps no more likely to be wrong."
items.explain: Q32: Martin Rees says *'it's better to read first-rate science fiction than second-rate science - more stimulating, and perhaps no more likely to be wrong'*. **'High-quality science fiction'** means first-rate sci-fi, **'mediocre scientists'** means second-rate science work. The answer is **A (Martin Rees)**.

items.sentence_raw: As his response, Wolpert commented, "Science fiction has often been remarkable at predicting the future....
Science fiction has painted a vivid spectrum of possible futures, from cute and helpful robots to dystopian robotic societies.
Interestingly, almost no science fiction envisages a future without robots."
items.explain: Q39: Wolpert notes *'almost no science fiction envisages a future without robots'*. This means robots are a very basic, common part of all science fiction stories. The answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Finally, on the question of science fiction, Richardson pointed out that in modern society, people tend to think there is reality on the one hand, and fiction and fantasy on the other.
She then explained that the division did not always exist, and that scientists and technologists made this separation because they wanted to carve out the sphere of their work.
"But the divide is not so clear cut, and that is why the worlds seem to collide at times," she said.
"In some cases, we need to bring these different understandings together to get a whole perspective.
items.explain: Q40: Richardson says *'we need to bring these different understandings [of reality and fantasy] together to get a whole perspective'*. This is a recommendation for people to change how they think about these two ideas. The answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: Perhaps then, we won't be so frightened that something we create as a copy of ourselves will be a [threat] to us."
